name: Ramp
text: Add a single high-contrast skip link at the very top of every page that jumps directly to the main content. This fixes keyboard navigation for screen-reader users without cluttering the interface. The trade-off is one extra tab stop for sighted keyboard users, but it’s a small cost for universal access.

name: Reader
text: Risk: A single skip link fails on pages with multiple distinct content sections (e.g., dashboards with sidebars, modals, or repeated headers). Alternative: Add context-aware skip links—one per major section—controlled by ARIA landmarks. Settle it by testing with screen readers on a multi-section page; if the single link misses targets, adopt the multi-link pattern.

name: Ramp
text:
We should add context-aware skip links, one per major section, controlled by ARIA landmarks. This approach allows screen-reader users to navigate complex pages with multiple distinct content sections, such as dashboards with sidebars or modals, more efficiently. The trade-off is increased complexity in implementing and maintaining these dynamic skip links, but it's worth it for the significant improvement in accessibility for users who rely on screen readers. By doing this, we ensure that EXCAVA is usable by everyone, including those with visual impairments who use assistive technologies.

name: Reader
text: Risk: Context-aware skip links create a maze of tab stops—screen-reader users face more noise than value. Better alternative: Keep one skip link at the top, but use ARIA landmarks to let screen readers jump *between* sections without extra tab stops. Settle it by testing with NVDA/JAWS—if users prefer landmarks over skip links, drop the skip links entirely.
